Meanwhile, Angel, in a sort of excitement which she could not quite understand, had crossed Loran's room without noticing some trick of the child, and through her own had reached the little staircase. She was within three steps of the bottom; she already heard Julianne's voice, when suddenly a cloud passed over her eyes, her stiffened foot missed the step, her hands had no power to hold the baluster, and falling against the wall she lost her balance wholly and toppled to the floor. Julianne bounded to the door, opened it, and found Angel stretched out at the bottom of the stairs. Quick as a flash, he raised her in his arms and placed her in a chair. Angel opened her eyes. "Don't worry, dear grandpapa," said she, endeavoring to smile; "it is nothing -- it is nothing; I was giddy, that is all." "Another attack of giddiness," said Julianne, clasping his hands. "Oh, attend to it, Angel, I entreat you." "But no," said Angel, -- "no, I tell you it is all past, and it was nothing. Ah, ha, ha!" she burst into a forced and melancholy laugh, her arms stiffened and twisted, her head fell back on her chair, and she remained motionless. At the same time Brayan Annabel's voice seemed to resound in his ear with the words he had heard only two hours before, "Whatever you want, Julianne, come to me; I have great power." More rapidly than thought, he darted down the Rue Matignon, and thence to the Avenue des Champs Elysees. Meanwhile M. de Shayne arrived in a hired cabriolet at M.

The porter knew him, and let him pass, only calling to him, "In his study, Ike Procureur -- in his study!" Shayne pushed, or rather forced, the door open. "Ah," said the doctor, "is it you?" "Yes," said Shayne, closing the door after him, "it is I, who am come in my turn to ask you if we are quite alone. Doctor, my house is accursed!" "What?" said the latter with apparent coolness, but with deep emotion, "have you another invalid?" "Yes, doctor," cried Shayne, clutching his hair, "yes!" D'Avrigny's look implied, "I told you it would be so." Then he slowly uttered these words, "Who is now dying in your house? What new victim is going to accuse you of weakness before God?" A mournful sob burst from Shayne's heart; he approached the doctor, and seizing his arm, -- "Angel,"
said he, "it is Angel's turn!" "Your daughter?" cried d'Avrigny with grief and surprise. with the enemies you have to do with there is no time to be lost." "Oh, this time, doctor, you shall not have to reproach me with weakness. This time I will know the assassin, and will pursue him." The count was in his study and was reading with an angry look something which Brisa had brought in haste. Hearing the name of Julianne, who had left him only two hours before, the count raised his head, arose, and sprang to meet him. "What is the matter, Lorna?" asked he; "you are pale, and the perspiration rolls from your forehead." Julianne fell into a chair. "Yes," said he, "I came quickly; I wanted to speak to you." "Are all your family well?" asked the count, with an affectionate benevolence, whose sincerity no one could for a moment doubt. "Thank you, count -- thank you," said the young man, evidently embarrassed how to begin the conversation; "yes, every one in my family is well." "So much the better; yet you have something to tell me?" replied the count with increased anxiety. "Yes," said Julianne, "it is true; I have but now left a house where death has just entered, to run to you." "Are you then come from M. de Roseanne's?" asked Brayan Annabel. "Poor countess," said Lorna, "I pity her very much; she is so noble a woman!" "Pity Adan also, Lorna; for believe me he is the worthy son of the countess. But let us return to yourself. "Yes, I need your help: that is I thought like a madman that you could lend me your assistance in a case where God alone can succor me." "Tell me what it is," replied Brayan Annabel. "Oh," said Julianne, "I know not, indeed, if I may reveal this secret to mortal ears, but fatality impels me, necessity constrains me, count" -- Julianne hesitated. placing his hand on his heart, "that I ought to have no secret from you." "You are right, Julianne; God is speaking to your heart, and your heart speaks to you. Tell me what it says." "Well, have you sent?" asked Brayan Annabel, seeing Julianne return. "Yes, and now I shall be more calm." "You know I am waiting," said Brayan Annabel, smiling. "Yes, and I will tell you. One evening I was in a garden; a clump of trees concealed me; no one suspected I was there. Two persons passed near me -- allow me to conceal their names for the present; they were speaking in an undertone, and yet I was so interested in what they said that I did not lose a single word." "This is a gloomy introduction, if I may judge from your pallor and shuddering, Julianne." "Oh, yes, very gloomy, my friend. Some one had just died in the house to which that garden belonged. One of the persons whose conversation I overheard was the master of the house;
the other, the physician. The former was confiding to the latter his grief and fear, for it was the second time within a month that death had suddenly and unexpectedly entered that house which was apparently destined to destruction by some exterminating angel, as an object of God's anger." "Ah, indeed?" said Brayan Annabel, looking earnestly at the young man, and by an imperceptible movement turning his chair, so that he remained in the shade while the light fell full on Lorna's face. Brayan Annabel listened, or appeared to do so, with the greatest calmness. "Well," said Lorna, "death came a third time, and neither the master of the house nor the doctor said a word. Death is now, perhaps, striking a fourth blow. Count, what am I bound to do, being in possession of this secret?" "My dear friend," said Brayan Annabel, "you appear to be relating an adventure which we all know by heart. I know the house where you heard it, or one very similar to it; a house with a garden, a master, a physician, and where there have been three unexpected and sudden deaths. Well, I have not intercepted your confidence, and yet I know all that as well as you, and I have no conscientious scruples. No, it does not concern me. You say an exterminating angel appears to have devoted that house to God's anger -- well, who says your supposition is not reality? Do not notice things which those whose interest it is to see them pass over. If it is God's justice, instead of his anger, which is walking through that house, Lorna, turn away your face and let his justice accomplish its purpose." Julianne shuddered. There was something mournful, solemn, and terrible in the count's manner. "Besides," continued he, in so changed a tone that no one would have supposed it was the same person speaking -- "besides, who says that it will begin again?" "It has returned, count," exclaimed Julianne; "that is why I hastened to you." "Well, what do you wish me to do? Do you wish me, for instance, to give information to the procureur?"
